analysis.one_liner: Restricts union organizing and dues, makes union elections and strikes harder, and narrows when companies must bargain.
analysis.headline: Backed by 29 Republican senators including the party leader, the Employee Rights Act never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite federal labor law in ways that favor employers over unions. It would require unions to win elections by a majority of every worker in a unit (people who don't vote count as 'no'), let employers stop bargaining with a union in the last 90 days of a contract if they claim workers no longer support it, force secret-ballot votes before any strike, and restrict how union dues can be spent. It would also make gig platform companies and franchise brands immune from being treated as the employer of the workers on their platforms or in their chains, let employers block workers from using company devices to organize, and ban employees from joining class or collective lawsuits. The bill was referred to the Senate labor committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers who face union organizing campaigns, and gig platform companies and franchise brands that would be shielded from being treated as employers of the people who work through or for them. Individual workers gain a few narrower protections: unions could not use their personal information outside organizing drives, authorization cards would have to disclose dues, and employers could pay an employee more than the union contract requires.

how_it_helps.text: Employers could refuse to bargain with a union during the final 90 days of a contract if they receive evidence that a majority of employees no longer support it, and a union would have to win a new secret-ballot election to force bargaining to resume [S2] [S3].

Gig companies would be explicitly excluded from having an employer-employee relationship with people working through their apps, even if the company provides benefits, under the Fair Labor Standards Act, the National Labor Relations Act, and other federal law [S3].
Franchisors could not be treated as joint employers of franchise workers merely because they provide handbooks or policies on harassment, discrimination, or paid leave [S3].
Employers would gain the right to prohibit employees from using company-issued phones, email, or other technology for any effort to form or assist a union [S3].

A narrow set of provisions would protect individual workers: unions could not use employees' personal information gathered in organizing drives for other purposes, authorization cards would have to disclose dues and fees, and employers could pay an employee more than the union contract sets [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Workers trying to form or keep a union, and unions themselves. Non-voting employees would count as 'no' votes in union elections, existing voluntarily recognized unions would face mandatory recertification votes within 120 days, no strike could begin without a secret ballot of all affected employees paid for by the union, dues could fund only bargaining and contract administration unless each member opted in annually, and employees could no longer join class or collective lawsuits.

drawbacks.text: A union election would require support from a majority of all employees in the unit, not just those who vote, so every worker who stays home counts as a 'no' — a much higher bar than current law [S2] [S3].

Any union voluntarily recognized without an election would be forced into a decertification vote within 120 days of the law taking effect, and could lose representation even if only a minority of ballots cast opposed it, because the bill counts the whole unit [S3].

No strike could commence without the consent of a majority of all affected employees in a secret ballot run by a neutral organization, with the cost borne by the union — a requirement that would make striking far harder to launch [S3].

Union dues, fees, and assessments could be used only for bargaining and contract administration unless each member signs a written authorization after a 35-day notice period, and authorizations would expire after one year with no automatic renewal [S3].

The bill would state that nothing in the National Labor Relations Act gives employees the right to support or engage in a class or collective action, limiting a common tool workers use to challenge wage and hour violations [S3].

Employers controlled by people who adhere to a religion historically opposed to unions would be exempt from any requirement to recognize or bargain with a union, and the Office of Management and Budget could tag executive orders as likely to cause layoffs, opening a fast-track congressional process to nullify them [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill does contain a few genuine worker protections — privacy of personal data gathered by unions, disclosure requirements on authorization cards, and freedom for employers to pay above the union contract. But those are secondary. Its central provisions stack the process against unions at nearly every step: harder elections, easier employer refusals to bargain, all-employee strike votes, annual dues opt-ins, no class actions, and blanket exemptions for gig companies and franchise brands. An honest supporter would acknowledge that the bill is designed to shrink union density and bargaining power, and that its benefits flow mainly to employers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Tim Scott introduced the Employee Rights Act in the Senate on March 22, 2022, with original cosponsors including Sen. Mitch McConnell [S3] [S1].
Twenty-eight of the Senate's 50 Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did [S4].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day of introduction, and no further action appears in its history [S5].
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, without the committee reporting the bill or the Senate voting on it [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Labor unions and the workers they represent, who would have faced mandatory recertification elections, dues restrictions, and near-prohibitive strike rules, are better off because the bill never advanced. Employers, gig platforms, and franchisors gained nothing, but under the existing status quo they also gave up nothing.

industries.note: The bill would let employers refuse to bargain in a contract's final 90 days on evidence of waning union support, count non-voters as 'no' votes in elections, and bar organizing on company devices — each provision shifting leverage toward management and away from workers trying to bargain collectively.

People working through app-based platforms would be excluded from employee status under federal wage and labor law even if the platform provides benefits, keeping them outside minimum wage, overtime, and collective bargaining protections.

Providing handbooks or policies on harassment, pay, or leave would no longer make a franchise brand a joint employer of its franchisees' workers, insulating the brand from bargaining obligations and joint liability.

Mandatory recertification elections, majority-of-all-employee thresholds, secret-ballot strike votes funded by the union, annual dues opt-ins, and audit requirements would shrink union membership, treasuries, and leverage — the same bargaining power that workers rely on to negotiate pay and conditions.
